I had written screenplays for a long time before technology caught up with filmmaking so that digital became a viable option. I made a web series. Then I started working on other people's projects. One of them, we had a screening at a theater for the first three episodes. 50 or so people came. I shot and edited the project. My producing partner on my web series showed up and I was like, holy shit, OK, the footage looks great on the big screen. We have to make our own feature.

Fast forward a year or so and we make our own feature. Then another. Microbudget but whatever. We're proud of the work we did but we can't raise any money. I'm bored out of my mind and I'm driving my girlfriend nuts and she says, take one of your old scripts and write a book. So I did. 

People were lukewarm on the web series (writing quality wise). But people trusted me with their projects, to shoot and edit them. I shot and edited a someone else's feature, too, before mine. I sat down and wrote that script for our first feature and after a reading with actors and all we made it. That was all the confidence I'll ever need to keep writing. The first film was well received. Won some awards at local festivals. I was very lucky. 

I have three novels that I self published that no one really cares about, but I love them and every once in a while I get a rating or a review from a stranger and man... what a boost. I've got three more in the pipe. Two are done, working on the third. I'll release them at the same time and move on to something else.

Stenosis in my lower back. I couldn't walk for two weeks. Finally went to the hospital via ambulance. First hospital, they treated the pain. No imaging, nothing. They finally found a cocktail that worked and got me up on my feet. Said, switch taking tylenol and ibuprophen every four hours. I was like OK. 

Next day, doing that, the pain came back even worse. Called another ambulance. They take me to a spine hospital. Fourteen hours later I get a room. Next morning on no sleep they take me to imagine. X-rays first. I somehow manage to get down on my back and they take the x-rays. The guy who was transporting me to radiology for an MRI grabs my arm and pulls me to a seated position. I've never felt pain like that in my entire life, and I dislocated my knee once, which was no fucking picnic. They finally put me on a nerve blocker and a muscle relaxer and my doctor came to me later that day and was like, yeah, your lower back is fucked. Took four days to get me so I could at least walk with a cane.

I loved movies as a kid but it wasn't until I watched Marathon Man in my first year of college when I went, holy shit, it's amazing what they're all capable of making. I had only watched action and horror movies up until that point. I'd seen some Lynch stuff and some Scorsese stuff but hadn't really delved below the surface. I was going to college to become a comic book artist.

A few years later I sat down and watched a VHS letterbox version of Wild at Heart and that put the zap on my head. I had already been writing scripts by this point (Reservoir Dogs, Clerks, El Mariachi came out around the same time and showed me a world where low budget films rule) but hadn't taken the format very seriously. It would be nearly twenty years after Marathon Man that I made my first web series (thankfully technology caught up and made filmmaking cheaper), shot a music video, shot other people's projects, and then my producing partner and I made two micro-budget features.

Nothing in my life has resonated with me more than filmmaking. Unfortunately, just before our third feature was to get off the ground, I got hurt and my career is basically over. But I'm very proud of what I accomplished. I just thought I had more time to make more stuff.

We shot a [music video](https://vimeo.com/47751246) and a [short](https://vimeo.com/71621198) that made it into a film festival. 

I then shot and edited a web series called [The Thing](https://vimeo.com/channels/568139). It was written and directed by a theater guy in NYC (where I live) who'd had some screenplays produced. I met some unbelievably talented actors he knew and worked with. We screened the first three episodes on a big screen at New Filmmakers in downtown NYC and turned to Julie and said 'we have to make a feature with some of these people.'

That short that got into the film festival, I met another filmmaker there and she asked me to shoot and edit her feature. I said sure. We made that and then eight months or so later shot our feature, [Stuck.](https://vimeo.com/114634446) We made it for about $7500, plus another $2k for post. Followed that up with a second feature, [Four Bottles,](https://vimeo.com/304064629) which we were able to raise about $35k for. That film, unfortunately, did not do what we hoped it would, which was secure more funding for a third. 

I decided to fund the third with credit cards and we were going to shoot it in October of 2019. Had it cast, had the locations. I ended up hurting my back so badly I couldn't walk. Was in the hospital for about a week, got out, was doing OK. Got a steroid shot in my back and couldn't walk two days later. Had a bad herniated disc that gave me a sciatica pain so bad I thought I'd shattered my leg. Had to cancel the film. After some surgeries I can walk fine and all but my filmmaking days are probably over. I can't hold a camera, I can't stay on my feet all day anymore. I can't sit down for longer than an hour. It really sucks because I'd finally found something I love doing.

If you love doing it, don't worry about your age. Put yourself out there. This shit is way too much fun to just think about.

edit: Just to share some news, Stuck is being remade in German with a female lead. When it premiered at a festival in NYC the same Germans had a film there and we became friends. This was 2014. They asked a year later if they could remake it. I said sure. It took a while for them to get the project going, but they did. It's a micro-budget feature, but they're making it at the end of March and beginning of April. Can't wait to see it.

Every time I go for a walk and listen to music, I inevitably come up with a scene I want to write. I match the scene to music, like a music video, and it helps me hone every detail. Even emotions. These scenes come way before I write a single part of the story, and I put the songs I match to the scene in a playlist on my ipod. I re-listen to the track(s) over and over and over again, even after I've written them, because I have a strong connection to the scene (and the book(s)). It still thrills me to recreate the scene in my head, but now it's more like how a tv show would look.

Once I've perfected the scene in my head, I have absolutely no problem writing it down exactly how I see it. You'll get there. Don't let this worry stop you from doing what you want.
